title: Trump's Saudi Arabia Trip — \B Arms Deal
description_short: Trump's Saudi Arabia Trip — \B Arms Deal
description_medium: Trump visited Saudi Arabia in May 2025 on his first major foreign trip of his second term, announcing a \ billion investment framework and a massive arms sale package. Critics immediately noted that Trump's family business had ongoing financial ties to Saudi sovereign wealth funds, including a golf tournament deal and real estate ventures worth hundreds of millions. No conditions were attached to the arms deals regarding human rights or the Jamal Khashoggi killing. Democrats called for an emoluments clause investigation.
description_long: The Guardian reported that the United States and Saudi Arabia announced a $142 billion arms sales agreement during Donald Trump’s May 2025 Gulf tour. The White House said the package involved more than a dozen U.S. defense companies and covered areas including air force, space, missile defense, border security and maritime capabilities. Separately, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman pledged $600 billion in U.S. investments and purchases, including data-center, energy and aircraft deals. These are distinct announcements: the $142 billion figure refers to the arms sales agreement, while $600 billion was the wider investment pledge. The Guardian describes the visit’s emphasis on commercial agreements but does not provide the final contract terms, identify human-rights conditions attached to individual sales or document the family-business connections asserted in the populated medium. The source therefore clarifies the malformed amount and the reported package without establishing the entry’s conflict-of-interest or human-rights claims. Signed agreements, conditions attached to arms transfers and records identifying the Trump family’s relevant financial interests would be needed to assess those questions.
notes: The Guardian reports a $142 billion arms-sales agreement and a separate $600 billion investment pledge during Trump's May 2025 visit. The populated medium has a malformed dollar figure and claims about family business ties and absent human-rights conditions that the linked report does not establish; it is preserved verbatim. Contract terms and company-level records are needed.

title: Trump Tower Moscow Negotiations Secretly Continued During 2016 Campaign
description_short: Trump Tower Moscow Negotiations Secretly Continued During 2016 Campaign
description_medium: Michael Cohen told a federal court in November 2018 that discussions about a proposed Trump Tower in Moscow continued during the 2016 presidential campaign. Cohen, who had worked for Donald Trump, said he had discussed the project with Russian contacts and had lied to Congress when he gave an earlier timeline. The proposal did not become a completed tower, and reports that a $50 million penthouse might be offered to Vladimir Putin do not establish that an offer was made.
description_long: In November 2018, Michael Cohen admitted that negotiations over a proposed Trump Tower in Moscow continued into the 2016 presidential campaign, contradicting the shorter timeline he had previously given Congress. Cohen had served as Donald Trump’s lawyer and fixer. The project would have required Russian government approval, and Cohen said he had discussed it with people connected to the Kremlin. He pleaded guilty to lying to Congress about the negotiations’ duration. The supplied account says the project team discussed offering Vladimir Putin a $50 million penthouse, but it does not establish that an offer was made or accepted. Nor does the continued negotiation by itself show that the Russian government approved the project or that it changed campaign policy. The disclosure mattered because Trump was campaigning while his company pursued a major development whose progress depended on Russian approval, even as he publicly minimized his Russia business ties. The account documents the timeline and Cohen’s plea while keeping the proposed project and uncompleted offer distinct from a finished transaction.
notes: The AP source returned HTTP 403. The supplied synopsis identifies continued negotiations, Cohen's guilty plea for lying to Congress about timing, and discussion of a possible penthouse. The account treats the building and offer as proposals, not completed transactions.

title: Threats To Invoke Insurrection Act
description_medium: Amid nationwide protests following the murder of George Floyd, President Trump threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act to deploy active-duty U.S. military troops against American citizens. He demanded that state governors aggressively dominate the protesters. This authoritarian escalation threatened core First Amendment rights and civilian control of the military.
notes: The supplied synopsis and linked transcript request describe a threat to invoke the Insurrection Act amid protests after George Floyd's murder, but the transcript could not be accessed. The exact statement, audience, statutory conditions, and whether any invocation or deployment followed are needed for a useful long account.

title: Steve Bannon Indicted for Contempt of Congress
description_short: Steve Bannon Indicted for Contempt of Congress
description_medium: On November 12, 2021, Steve Bannon was indicted by a federal grand jury for contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with subpoenas from the January 6 Committee. Bannon, claiming executive privilege despite not working in the government, was later convicted and sentenced to four months in prison.
description_long: On November 12, 2021, a federal grand jury indicted Steve Bannon on two counts of contempt of Congress after he refused to comply with subpoenas from the House committee investigating the January 6 attack. The subpoenas sought testimony and documents about the committee’s inquiry. Bannon claimed executive privilege, although he was a private citizen and no longer served in the government when the committee sought his cooperation. The indictment began a criminal case; it did not itself determine whether his privilege argument was valid or establish guilt. Bannon was later convicted on both counts and sentenced to four months in prison. Those are later procedural outcomes, distinct from the indictment announced in this entry. The case tested Congress’s ability to enforce subpoenas through criminal referrals and Justice Department prosecution. The available account does not establish that every noncompliance dispute is criminal or resolve broader legal questions about executive privilege. It records the specific refusal, indictment, and later result while keeping each stage of the proceeding separate.
notes: The supplied Justice Department source and synopsis identify the indictment date, subpoena refusal, privilege claim, later conviction, and four-month sentence. The account distinguishes the indictment from the later verdict and avoids extending the result to other privilege disputes.

title: Electoral College Certified Despite Protests and Faithless Electors
description_short: Electoral College Certified Despite Protests and Faithless Electors
description_medium: On December 19, 2016, electors met in their state capitals to cast Electoral College votes. Donald Trump received 304 electoral votes, two fewer than the 306 he had been expected to receive, as two Republican electors voted for someone else. Seven electors cast faithless votes overall. Congress counted the votes on January 6, 2017, and completed certification after attempted objections lacked a Senate co-sponsor.
description_long: The Electoral College met on December 19, 2016, to cast the votes that determine the president and vice president. Donald Trump received 304 electoral votes, two fewer than the 306 pledged by his expected slate, after two Republican electors voted for other candidates. Five Democratic electors also departed from their pledged votes, leaving seven faithless electors in total, the most since 1872. That vote was a state-level Electoral College step, not Congress’s certification of the result. Congress met in joint session on January 6, 2017, to count the electoral votes. Several House Democrats attempted to object, but their objections could not proceed without a senator joining them. Vice President Joe Biden presided over the count and ruled the objections out of order when the required support was absent. The sequence shows both the independent votes cast by electors and the formal congressional count. The objections did not change the outcome, and the Electoral College’s votes were certified through the constitutional process.
notes: The supplied chronology distinguishes the electors' December 19 vote from Congress's January 6 count. The National Archives page is the official reference for the electoral process; the account does not conflate the two certification stages.
